summary: Describes requirements for, and use of, the GMPLS control plane to support Virtual Concatenation and the Link Capacity Adjustment Scheme. These layer 1 inverse multiplexing mechanisms let the capacity of a group of channels be resized without interruption, in optical transport and SONET/SDH networks.

plainLanguage.summary: Virtual concatenation lets several small data channels act as one big one. This explains how a network's control software sets that up and changes its size without cutting off traffic.

questions: hitless resizing of inverse multiplex group
how does gmpls signal virtual concatenation
subtitle: How GMPLS signaling sets up and resizes virtually concatenated optical and SONET/SDH channel groups, including diversely routed ones.

tldr.problem: Virtual concatenation (VCAT) bonds several TDM signals into one bigger pipe, but the existing GMPLS procedures only handled members that all follow one route inside a single LSP.
tldr.mechanism: VCAT calls, built on the RSVP-TE call procedures, group several control plane LSPs into one VCG, and a new VCAT TLV in the CALL_ATTRIBUTES object carries signal type, member count, LCAS requirement, an action and a VCG ID.
tldr.outcome: Members can be pre-established, shared between groups, diversely routed and added or removed, with LCAS in the data plane making resizing hitless. The RFC updates RFC 4606.

today: RFC 6344 is a Proposed Standard and is not obsoleted by any later RFC. It updates RFC 4606.

sections.title: What VCAT and LCAS Are
sections.content:
Generalized Multi-Protocol Label Switching (GMPLS) automates control of several switching technologies, including SONET, SDH, OTN and PDH. Virtual Concatenation (VCAT) is a time-division multiplexing (TDM) byte-striping inverse multiplexing method: it lets a group of server signals act as one connection, so the bandwidth can be sized to fit the client. The companion Link Capacity Adjustment Scheme (LCAS) adds hitless dynamic resizing and fast graceful degradation when faults occur.

To get the full benefit, GMPLS signaling needs extensions that can set up diversely routed signals belonging to one VCAT group. This document updates the procedures of RFC 4606 for that purpose. Its scope is limited to cases where every member signal of a group is controlled by the mechanisms described here and in related RFCs. Groups where some members are controlled by a management plane or proprietary control plane are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Several small channels can be tied together to act like one big channel, and a helper protocol lets you add or remove channels smoothly. This RFC teaches the network's control software how to manage that.

sections.title: Scenarios and Requirements
sections.content:
VCAT and LCAS are data plane interface capabilities. A router may have interfaces that are VCAT-capable but not LCAS-capable, and others that are neither. The RFC lists six member configurations, built from two choices: fixed or dynamic bandwidth, and co-routed (all members take the same sequence of nodes over links of similar delay), diversely routed (at least two subsets, link-disjoint over at least one link) or member sharing (members drawn from a common pool without tearing down and setting up connections). A member can belong to only one group at a time.

GMPLS procedures are REQUIRED both with and without LCAS, and SHOULD be identical. Signaling for LCAS-capable interfaces MUST support all scenarios with no traffic loss, while signaling for non-LCAS interfaces MUST support the fixed scenarios. Signaling must carry the member signal type, the total number of members, and an identification of the group and its members. Members SHOULD be allowed to be set up before use and to outlive their group.
sections.plainLanguage: Some groups never change size and some grow and shrink. Some pipes take the same road and some take different roads. The control software has to handle all of those, with or without the smooth-resizing helper.

sections.title: Data and Control Plane Concepts
sections.content:
The RFC defines a few terms used throughout:

  • VCG: the group of data plane server-layer signals that provides the bandwidth of the virtual concatenation link connection.
  • VCG member: one data plane signal in the VCG. A data plane LSP is an individual member.
  • Member set: one or more members set up by the same signaling exchange; all members of a set follow the same route.
  • Control plane LSP: a control plane entity that can control multiple data plane LSPs; here it is equivalent to a member set.
  • Call: a control plane mechanism that associates endpoints and possibly key transit points.
sections.plainLanguage: A group is the whole bundle, a member is one strand, and a call is the paperwork tying strands to the right bundle.

sections.title: One Member Set: A Single LSP
sections.content:
A group made of one member set (fixed or dynamic co-routed) already works with the procedures in RFC 4606, using its Number of Virtual Components (NVC) field. This section is informational and does not modify that RFC; if they conflict, RFC 4606 wins.

The example is a VC-4-7v group of 7 virtually concatenated VC-4s. In one-shot setup, an RSVP-TE Path message carries elementary signal 6 and NVC 7, and the Generalized Label is an ordered list of 32-bit timeslot identifiers, one per member, in payload order rather than physical order. In incremental setup, NVC starts at 1 and each successful Path and Resv round increments it and appends one more timeslot identifier; LCAS may then add the new member in the data plane.

To remove members, LCAS first takes them out of service, then NVC is decremented and their identifiers are dropped from the label. Interfaces without LCAS cannot do this: removing a component is detected as a member failure and fails the whole group. Tearing down the entire group deletes the LSP in one step using RFC 3473 procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: With one road for all strands, you can build the bundle all at once or add one strand at a time. Taking a strand away smoothly needs the helper protocol; without it, the whole bundle breaks.

sections.title: The VCAT TLV
sections.content:
Diversely routed members need several control plane LSPs, because RFC 4606 keeps all components of one LSP on the same link. This document updates it by using the call procedures of RFC 4974: a VCG is made of one or more VCAT calls, each holding control plane LSPs, each controlling co-routed data plane connections. The VCG ID is kept separate from the call ID so that calls (with their LSPs) can be moved between groups for member sharing.

Group-level information travels in a new VCAT TLV inside the CALL_ATTRIBUTES object (RFC 6001) of a Notify message. The Notify message is targeted and need not follow the LSP path, so the call does not depend on member signaling. The TLV is 12 bytes long and carries:

  • Signal Type (16 bits): one type per group that MUST never change during its life.
  • Number of Members (16 bits): the current total in the VCG (not just the call), updated as it changes.
  • LCR (LCAS Required, 2 bits): 0 required, 1 desired, 2 not supported; MUST NOT change during the group's life.
  • Action (8 bits): the relationship between call and VCG.
  • VCG ID (16 bits): MUST NOT change over the life of a VCG but MAY change over the life of a call.
sections.plainLanguage: A small form is attached to the call saying what kind of strands, how many, whether the smooth-resizing helper is needed, what to do now, and the bundle's name.

sections.title: Procedures for Multiple Member Sets
sections.content:
VCAT calls and their LSPs follow RFC 4974, with a CALL_ATTRIBUTES object holding the VCAT TLV added. The Action field drives what happens:

  • New call and VCG together (Action 1): LSPs are then added until the member count in the TLV is reached.
  • Call without a VCG (Action 0): pre-establishes connections. A pool of such calls can later be attached to a VCG, but a call MUST NOT contain members used in more than one VCG.
  • Associate an existing call with a VCG (Action 1 plus the VCG ID): the Number of Members MUST equal the sum of all LSPs in the VCG. The sender must be ready for an error response, since a node may limit its number of VCGs.
  • Remove the association (Action 3): the VCG ID and member count are ignored. When no calls remain associated, the VCG is considered torn down.
  • Change bandwidth (Action 2): before any other change, a Notify MUST be sent for each call in the VCG with the member count anticipated after the change. If an error occurs, the count is reverted and the increase aborted. Then LSPs are added or removed, or a call is associated or dissociated.

With LCAS, the data plane adds or drops members per G.7042. Without LCAS across LSPs, data plane coordination across member sets is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: To change the bundle, you first announce the new size to everyone, and only then add or remove strands. If anything goes wrong, the announced size goes back to the old one.

sections.title: Error Conditions
sections.content:
Setting up a VCAT call or associating it with a VCG can be denied. These errors fall under RSVP error code 39 (VCAT Call Management), with seven values from 1 to 7, covering an unsupported signal type, unsupported LCAS option, too many VCGs, too many members, an LSP type incompatible with the call, an unknown LCR value and an unknown or unsupported Action.

Any failure in call or LSP establishment MUST be treated as a failure of the whole VCG, and MAY trigger deletion of the calls and LSPs associated with it.
sections.plainLanguage: If something about one strand cannot work, the network treats the whole bundle as failed and may take it all down.

sections.title: IANA and Security
sections.content:
IANA assigned VCAT TLV value 4 in the Call Attributes TLV registry and created RSVP error code 39 with the seven values above. It also created two registries, each allocated by IETF Review: VCAT elementary signals (range 0 to 65535, value 0 reserved) and VCAT VCG operation actions (range 0 to 255).

The document introduces no new signaling messages and does not change the relationship between adjacent routers in the control plane. Its use of Notify and ADMIN_STATUS follows RFC 3473 as modified by RFC 4974. One note: call information on diversely routed LSPs, if intercepted, may reveal that they belong to one VCAT group taking different routes, and that the call wants more reliability. See RFC 5920 for GMPLS security in general.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is added that attackers could aim at, but someone listening in might learn that the strands belong together and that someone wants extra safety.
